doc.title: Javon Jackson interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 3, 2020 [interview 2 of 2]

title: Teaching online: lessons, courses and ensembles
summary: Online teaching works for private lessons and his business course but is hard for ensembles; he considers pre-recorded rhythm sections.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: Did you, as the head of the school, the jazz department, have a say in what methods you would try to keep working with the students when everyone had to vacate campus?
Right. It was basically a university mandate that everything would occur online. So we took on that same process like most universities and institutions are doing throughout the United States.
What’s your experience been with it? Has it been difficult?

I found it to be okay actually in a one-on-one situation where you’re doing private lessons it’s much the same except that individual is not in the same room as you. But beyond that we’re still able to have conversations. They’re able to play something. I’m able to give a response in terms of some feedback or support, and we can still develop with coursework. There’s a business course that I teach that is not necessarily a problem because we have Zoom in this same manner, and one person is normally speaking at a time. The tough situation comes when it pertains to ensembles where we’re used to having everyone perform together, interact in real time, interface, have conversation, definitely very difficult because now you’re in a situation where someone has to play something and then that might get layered on top, almost like in the way if you’re doing a
recording out in a studio. But the students aren’t necessarily able to grasp that interaction that you feel when you’re presenting as a group, in person.
Yes, do you — this would be like looking into the future — do you anticipate that there might be more emphasis on using this even when it’s not necessary?

Well I mean definitely for health reasons, until there’s a vaccine for what we’re currently going through, there’s going to have to be a way for us to find the opportunity for students to get the best experience they can through this platform. So whether it means having a pre-recorded rhythm section, bass, drums and piano or guitar as part of that rhythm section, and they create the bottom if you will, or the palette for the rest of the composition. It might have to occur like that for a while. I’m sure, there are certain platforms I’m told where you’re actually able to play at the same time with headphones and very much in the same way as if you’re in a studio. I just haven’t become acutely aware of them to be able to implement them myself, but my guess is if it has to happen in the next month or so I’ll do some research, and the students are probably so far ahead of me they’re aware of how this can occur anyway.

Yeah. Sometimes the little bit of experience I had with it finishing a semester was comical because sometimes the students on the other end would be talking me through the tech issues and I suppose it’s a good learning experience for us that aren’t that familiar with it or comfortable.
